# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** By "biological father" I mean a male parent who supplies the begetting seed. The standard reading is that Jesus Christ had a human mother, Mary, and no human male parent. Joseph was his legal and reputed father, not his begetter. His conception was "of the Holy Ghost."

## 1. The conception was out of the Holy Ghost, with no man involved

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, **before they came together**, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** Three Greek points carry this verse.
- *Prin ē sunelthein autous* (πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν αὐτούς: "before that they came together") fixes the time of the conception before any union of the couple.
- *En gastri echousa* (ἐν γαστρὶ ἔχουσα: "having in womb") describes the pregnancy.
- *Ek pneumatos hagiou* (ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου: "out of spirit holy") gives the source with *ek* (ἐκ: "out of"), the preposition of origin.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** *To gennēthen* (τὸ γεννηθέν: "the thing begotten/conceived") is the same verb family used of fathers begetting in the genealogy. Here the Holy Ghost is the stated source (*ek pneumatos*, "out of spirit").

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19 shows that Joseph, a "just man," did not regard the child as his own. He was "minded to put her away privily." The angel's message in verse 20 ("fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife") is what corrects him.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the Holy Ghost as the source of the conception. Joseph's reaction in 1:19 shows he had not begotten it. Together these exclude Joseph, and any other man, as begetter.

## 2. Matthew breaks his own "begat" pattern at the decisive point

**[L1]** Matthew 1:2–16 reads "Abraham begat Isaac... Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, **of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ**."

**[L2]** The verb for fathers is *egennēsen* (ἐγέννησεν: "begat"), active voice with a male subject, repeated through the list. In verse 16 it changes to *egennēthē* (ἐγεννήθη: "was begotten/born"), passive. The relative pronoun is *hēs* (ἧς: "of whom"), feminine singular, so it can refer only to Mary, not to Joseph (who is masculine). The list stops saying "Joseph begat Jesus" exactly where we would expect it.

**[L4]** The pattern is "A begat B" all the way down, and then Joseph is called only "the husband of Mary." The text exhibits the pattern ([L1] 1:2–16) and the lexical break ([L2] *egennēsen* to *egennēthē*, masculine to feminine). That break signals that Joseph did not beget Jesus.

## 3. Mary herself states she had not known a man

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *Epei andra ou ginōskō* (ἐπεὶ ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω: "since a man I know not"). The verb *ginōskō* (γινώσκω: "I know") is in the present tense and is the biblical idiom for sexual knowledge, as in Genesis 4:1, *yada'* (יָדַע: "he knew").

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall **overshadow** thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *Episkiasei* (ἐπισκιάσει: "will cast a shadow over") is the verb for the cloud covering at the transfiguration (Luke 9:34). It describes the presence and power of God, not a bodily union.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**[L2]** *Eginōsken* (ἐγίνωσκεν: "was knowing") is imperfect tense, a continued state. The negation covers the whole period up to the birth.

**[L3]** Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:25 are two independent witnesses to the same fact, Mary's and Joseph's, in two different gospels.

## 4. The old promise names a woman's seed and a woman's son

**[L1]** Genesis 3:15: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and **her seed**."

**[L2]** *Zar'ah* (זַרְעָהּ: "her seed") is unusual, because seed is normally reckoned through the male line.

**[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, **made of a woman**, made under the law."

**[L2]** *Genomenon ek gynaikos* (γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός: "coming to be out of a woman"). Paul names only the woman as the human source, and he writes *genomenon* (γενόμενον: "becoming/coming to be"), not the begetting verb.

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son"; Matthew 1:22–23 cites it as fulfilled.

**[L2]** The Hebrew is *ha'almah* (הָעַלְמָה: "the young woman," the maiden of marriageable age). Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (παρθένος: "virgin"), which is the inspired New Testament reading of the word. Matthew applies it to Mary, and Luke 1:27, 34 supports it.

**[L3]** The same line runs from Genesis 3:15 to Isaiah 7:14 to Galatians 4:4 to Matthew 1:23. Each names the woman, never a man, as the human source.

## 5. Joseph is "supposed" father, not begetter

**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (**as was supposed**) the son of Joseph."

**[L2]** *Enomizeto* (ἐνομίζετο: "was thought, was reckoned by custom") means that is how people thought of him. It does not say that is what he was.

**[L1]** Luke 2:48–49: Mary says, "Thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Jesus answers, "Wist ye not that I must be about **my Father's** business?"

**[L2]** *Tou patros mou* (τοῦ πατρός μου: "of my Father") is Jesus's own correction of "thy father" in the same exchange.

**[L1]** John 6:42: the people say, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" Their words record what the crowd believed. The text does not endorse it.

## 6. God's fatherhood is not biology by seed

**[L1]** John 4:24: "God is a Spirit." Luke 24:39: "a spirit hath not flesh and bones."

**[L1]** Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."

**[L2]** *Katērtisō* (κατηρτίσω: "you fitted/prepared") is a verb of preparing, not of begetting by seed.

**[L1]** John 1:14: "the Word was made flesh... the glory as of the only begotten of the Father."

**[L2]** *Monogenous* (μονογενοῦς: "only-born, one of a kind") marks a unique relation. In Luke 1:35 the title Son of God follows "therefore also" (*dio kai*, διὸ καί: "for which reason also") from the Holy Ghost's coming upon Mary.

**[L3]** John 4:24 and Luke 24:39 rule out a bodily, seed-supplying Father. Hebrews 10:5 and Luke 1:35 give the alternative: a body prepared, a conception by the Holy Ghost's power. The Father's fatherhood is therefore unique and not a matter of biological seed. So the question about a "biological father" gets the answer no.

## 7. Why Joseph's seed would have been a problem

**[L1]** Matthew 1:11–12 lists Jechonias in Joseph's line. **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30 says of Coniah (the same man): "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."

**[L1]** Romans 1:3: Christ was "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L1]** Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."

**[L4]** Matthew 1:11–12 puts Joseph in Jechonias's line, and Jeremiah 22:30 bars that line's seed from the throne. Romans 1:3 and Luke 1:32 say Christ has a Davidic descent and a Davidic throne. If Joseph had begotten Jesus, the one condition would defeat the other. The Davidic descent can run through Mary instead (Luke 3:23–31 traces the line through Nathan, David's son, not through Solomon), which fits Galatians 4:4. This is an inference from these verses, offered alongside the direct statements above and not instead of them.
